INTERVIEW STATEMENT - CHAD MCKENZIE

I am genuinely enthusiastic about using AI in technical education because it can turn a passive lesson into a much more active learning experience. A student can ask for another example, request a different explanation, compare two possible solutions, or explore why a command failed without waiting for the next class meeting. That immediate interaction can be incredibly valuable when someone is building confidence with unfamiliar technology.

In cloud and IT courses, I especially like the idea of treating AI as a troubleshooting partner. Students can use it to interpret an error message, generate test cases, outline a diagnostic path, or suggest questions they should investigate next. The important part is that they still verify the recommendation and understand the result. When we teach that habit explicitly, AI becomes a reason to think more carefully, not less.

I have also seen AI make projects more creative. Students who might have been hesitant to start can quickly brainstorm several approaches and then choose one to develop themselves. That momentum matters. A blank page can be intimidating, while a set of possibilities gives students something useful to evaluate and improve. It is rewarding to watch a student move from uncertainty to curiosity because the tool helped them take the first step.

Of course, instructors need clear expectations. Copying a generated answer without understanding it is not learning, and students should never assume that an AI response is correct. But those are teachable problems. We can design assessments that require explanation, demonstration, reflection, and verification. I would rather prepare students to use AI professionally than prohibit a technology they are likely to encounter after graduation. Overall, I see AI as practical, motivating, and full of opportunities for better learning when it is used responsibly.
